questions.stem: On coffee-shop Wi-Fi that Windows has classified as a Public network, a laptop can't receive incoming file-sharing connections. At the office, on the Domain network, the same laptop accepts them. Web browsing works in both places. Why?

options.text: Windows Defender Firewall applies the Public profile, which blocks inbound connections unless a rule allows them; outbound traffic is allowed by default
options.rationale: Correct: the active profile follows the network location.

options.text: The Public profile blocks all outbound traffic
options.rationale: Browsing works, so outbound traffic is allowed.

options.text: The firewall is turned off at the office
options.rationale: Nothing suggests that; the Domain profile simply has rules that allow file sharing.

options.text: The Public profile blocks every kind of traffic
options.rationale: Browsing still works, so not everything is blocked.

questions.explanation: Windows Defender Firewall is a built-in, host-based firewall with separate Domain, Private, and Public profiles. Inbound traffic is blocked unless a rule allows it, outbound is allowed by default, and the active profile depends on the network location.
questions.discriminator_tested: The active firewall profile depends on network location; inbound is blocked by default.

questions.stem: An administrator says: 'We set PowerShell's execution policy to Restricted, so attackers can't run PowerShell on our PCs.' What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: Execution policy is a safety setting, not a security boundary; it is easily bypassed, and attackers routinely abuse built-in scripting tools
options.rationale: Correct: this is 'living off the land', and execution policy doesn't stop it.

options.text: Nothing; Restricted makes PowerShell impossible to start
options.rationale: PowerShell still runs, and the policy can be bypassed, for example by passing commands directly.

options.text: Attackers never use PowerShell, so the setting is irrelevant
options.rationale: Attackers use PowerShell heavily.

options.text: Only batch files are a threat, so PowerShell needs no control
options.rationale: Every scripting tool can be misused.

questions.explanation: Scripting with PowerShell, batch, VBScript, or Python automates admin tasks, but attackers use the same tools ('living off the land'). PowerShell's execution policy is a safety setting, not a security boundary.
questions.discriminator_tested: Execution policy is a safety setting, not a security boundary.

questions.stem: Which two Windows security considerations reduce a workstation's attack surface? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use a standard user account for daily work
options.rationale: Correct: malware runs with fewer rights.

options.text: Disable unused accounts and services
options.rationale: Correct: fewer ways in.

options.text: Make every user a local administrator to avoid prompts
options.rationale: This enlarges the attack surface.

options.text: Turn off antimalware to improve performance
options.rationale: This removes a protective layer.

options.text: Disable BitLocker on laptops
options.rationale: This exposes data if a laptop is stolen.

questions.explanation: Hardening Windows means daily use as a standard user, disabling unused accounts and services, running antimalware, and encrypting disks with BitLocker. The goal is a smaller attack surface with layered controls.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hardening reduces attack surface with layered controls.

questions.stem: A user belongs to two groups that have NTFS permissions on the same folder: Sales has Allow Read, and Projects has Allow Modify. There are no Deny entries. What is the user's effective NTFS access?

options.text: Modify
options.rationale: Correct: NTFS permissions from different groups add together.

options.text: Read
options.rationale: Taking the most restrictive applies when combining share and NTFS permissions, not between NTFS groups.

options.text: No access, because the permissions conflict
options.rationale: Allow entries don't conflict; they add up.

options.text: Full control
options.rationale: Neither group grants Full control.

questions.explanation: NTFS permissions are cumulative across groups, so the user gets the union of Read and Modify, which is Modify. An explicit Deny would override an Allow, but there is none here.
questions.discriminator_tested: NTFS permissions are cumulative across groups; Deny overrides Allow.

questions.stem: A user logs on directly at a file server and opens a folder that is also shared on the network. Which permissions determine this user's access?

options.text: Only the NTFS permissions; share permissions are ignored for local access
options.rationale: Correct: share permissions apply only to network access.

options.text: Only the share permissions
options.rationale: Share permissions don't apply to someone logged on locally.

options.text: The more restrictive of the share and NTFS permissions
options.rationale: That rule applies to access over the network.

options.text: Neither; local users always have full access
options.rationale: NTFS permissions still apply.

questions.explanation: For local permissions (a user logged on at the machine), only NTFS permissions apply. Share permissions are ignored, because they affect only access over the network.
questions.discriminator_tested: Locally, only NTFS applies; share permissions are ignored.

questions.stem: A folder's share permissions give Everyone Read. Its NTFS permissions give the Marketing group Modify. A Marketing user opens the folder over the network. What is the user's effective access?

options.text: Read
options.rationale: Correct: over the network, the more restrictive of share and NTFS wins.

options.text: Modify
options.rationale: Share Read limits network access, even though NTFS allows Modify.

options.text: Full control
options.rationale: Neither layer grants Full control.

options.text: No access
options.rationale: Both layers allow at least Read.

questions.explanation: Share permissions (Read, Change, Full Control) apply only to network access. Combined with NTFS, the more restrictive of the two is the effective access.
questions.discriminator_tested: Over the network, effective access is the more restrictive of share and NTFS.

questions.stem: File 1, which has explicit NTFS permissions, is moved from D:\Projects to D:\Archive. File 2 is copied from D:\Projects to D:\Archive. What permissions does each file end up with?

options.text: File 1 keeps its permissions; File 2 takes the permissions of D:\Archive
options.rationale: Correct: a move within the same volume keeps permissions, and a copy inherits from the destination.

options.text: Both files keep their original permissions
options.rationale: A copy is a new file, so it inherits from the destination.

options.text: Both files take the permissions of D:\Archive
options.rationale: A move within the same volume keeps the file's permissions.

options.text: File 1 takes the destination's permissions; File 2 keeps its own
options.rationale: This reverses the rules.

questions.explanation: File permission inheritance logic: a copy takes the destination's permissions, a move within the same volume keeps its permissions, and a move to another volume takes the destination's.
questions.discriminator_tested: Copy takes the destination's permissions; a same-volume move keeps them.

questions.stem: An administrator creates a share named Payroll$ and calls it secure because it doesn't appear when users browse the network. Is it secure?

options.text: No: the $ only hides it from browsing, so anyone who knows the name can connect if the permissions allow; security comes from the share and NTFS permissions
options.rationale: Correct: hidden is not the same as protected.

options.text: Yes: a $ share is encrypted
options.rationale: The $ does not encrypt anything.

options.text: Yes: only administrators can ever open a $ share
options.rationale: Access depends on the permissions, not the name.

options.text: No, because $ shares use Telnet on TCP 23
options.rationale: File shares use SMB on TCP 445.

questions.explanation: Shared files and folders are published over SMB (TCP 445). A share name ending in $ only hides it from browsing; it doesn't secure it. Permissions do.
questions.discriminator_tested: A $ only hides a share; it doesn't secure it.

questions.stem: On the same Windows PC, an administrator and a standard user each try to install software. What does User Account Control show each of them?

options.text: The administrator sees a consent prompt (Yes/No); the standard user sees a credential prompt asking for an administrator's password
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Both see a credential prompt
options.rationale: Administrators only need to consent.

options.text: Neither sees a prompt
options.rationale: Installing software needs elevation, which triggers UAC.

options.text: The administrator sees no prompt; the standard user is simply refused
options.rationale: Administrators still run with a standard token until they consent, and standard users can supply admin credentials.

questions.explanation: UAC prompts before actions that need administrative rights. Administrators run with a standard token until they elevate, so they get a consent prompt; standard users get a credential prompt.
questions.discriminator_tested: UAC: admin = consent prompt; standard user = credential prompt.

questions.stem: What separates Windows Updates' monthly cumulative security updates from feature updates?

options.text: Monthly security updates, released on Patch Tuesday (the second Tuesday), fix vulnerabilities and quality issues; feature updates deliver a new version of the OS
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Feature updates contain only security fixes
options.rationale: Feature updates deliver a new OS version with new capabilities.

options.text: Monthly updates are optional new OS versions
options.rationale: Monthly updates fix vulnerabilities; new versions come as feature updates.

options.text: They are the same thing
options.rationale: They differ in both purpose and schedule.

questions.explanation: Windows Update delivers OS security, quality, and feature updates. Monthly cumulative security updates arrive on Patch Tuesday; feature updates deliver a new OS version.
questions.discriminator_tested: Monthly security updates (Patch Tuesday) vs feature updates (new OS version).

questions.stem: A Windows PC with every Windows Update installed is compromised through a known flaw in an outdated version of its third-party PDF reader. What does this show?

options.text: Third-party applications need their own patching process; Windows Update doesn't patch most of them
options.rationale: Correct: OS patching and application patching are separate jobs.

options.text: Windows Update must have failed
options.rationale: Windows Update worked; it just doesn't cover this application.

options.text: PDF readers can't be patched
options.rationale: Vendors release updates; they simply weren't applied.

options.text: A firmware update was missed
options.rationale: The flaw is in application software, not device firmware.

questions.explanation: Application patching is a separate process: third-party apps such as browsers, PDF readers, and runtimes need their own updates. Patching the OS doesn't patch most of them.
questions.discriminator_tested: OS patching doesn't patch most third-party apps.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates a device driver from firmware?

options.text: A driver is OS-side software, running in kernel mode, that lets the OS talk to hardware; firmware is code stored on the device itself
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Firmware runs inside the OS; drivers are stored on the device's chip
options.rationale: This reverses them.

options.text: They are the same thing
options.rationale: They live in different places and are updated separately.

options.text: Drivers run only in user mode and can't affect stability
options.rationale: Drivers run in kernel mode, which is why bad drivers can crash the system.

questions.explanation: Device drivers are software that lets the OS communicate with hardware, running in kernel mode. Firmware is code on the device itself. 64-bit Windows requires signed kernel drivers.
questions.discriminator_tested: Driver = OS-side kernel software; firmware = code on the device.

questions.stem: A Mac user downloads an app from a developer's website instead of the Mac App Store. Which macOS feature checks whether the app comes from an identified, notarized developer?

options.text: Gatekeeper
options.rationale: Correct: it controls apps from outside the store.

options.text: The App Store review process
options.rationale: That covers only apps distributed through the store.

options.text: UAC
options.rationale: UAC is a Windows feature.

options.text: The macOS application firewall
options.rationale: The firewall controls network connections, not where an app came from.

questions.explanation: The Mac App Store is Apple's reviewed, sandboxed distribution channel. Gatekeeper controls apps from outside the store by checking for identified or notarized developers.
questions.discriminator_tested: Gatekeeper covers apps from outside the store; the App Store is the curated source.

questions.stem: An Ubuntu server needs security updates for both the operating system and the packages installed from its repositories. Which tool updates both?

options.text: apt
options.rationale: Correct: Ubuntu's package manager updates the OS and repository-installed apps together.

options.text: macOS Software Update
options.rationale: That updates Macs.

options.text: Windows Update
options.rationale: That updates Windows.

options.text: chmod
options.rationale: chmod changes file permissions; it doesn't install updates.

questions.explanation: System updates on Linux come through the package manager: apt on Debian and Ubuntu, dnf or yum on Red Hat and Fedora. It updates the OS and repository-installed apps together; macOS updates come from Apple.
questions.discriminator_tested: A Linux package manager updates the OS and repo apps together.

questions.stem: Which sequence best reflects a sound patch management process?

options.text: Inventory, identify, evaluate and test, approve, deploy, verify, document
options.rationale: Correct: know what you have, test before production, then confirm and record.

options.text: Deploy, test, then take inventory
options.rationale: Testing must happen before deployment.

options.text: Identify, deploy to all production systems at once, document
options.rationale: This skips testing, approval, and verification.

options.text: Approve, deploy, then identify which patches are needed
options.rationale: You can't approve patches you haven't identified yet.

questions.explanation: Patch management is an ongoing process: inventory, identify, evaluate and test, approve, deploy, verify, and document. It is a managed process with a rollback plan, not a single update.
questions.discriminator_tested: Patch management is a managed process: test before production.

questions.stem: What separates the macOS application firewall from a Linux firewall managed with ufw?

options.text: macOS rules are set per application; Linux rules are based on ports and addresses, and ufw is a front-end to netfilter rather than a separate firewall
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: macOS rules are port-based; ufw rules are per application
options.rationale: This reverses the two.

options.text: ufw is a separate kernel firewall that replaces netfilter
options.rationale: ufw is a front-end that manages netfilter rules.

options.text: The macOS firewall is on by default and blocks all outbound traffic
options.rationale: The macOS application firewall is off by default and filters incoming connections.

questions.explanation: The macOS firewall is an application firewall, off by default, with per-application rules. Linux uses netfilter, managed through iptables/nftables or front-ends such as ufw and firewalld, with port- and address-based rules.
questions.discriminator_tested: macOS rules are per application; Linux rules are port/address-based; ufw is a front-end.

questions.stem:
'ls -l' shows:

-rwxr-x--- 1 alice devs 4096 Oct 3 report.sh

What can a member of the devs group (other than alice) do with this file, and what is its numeric mode?

options.text: Read and execute it, but not write to it; mode 750
options.rationale: Correct: the group bits are r-x (5), owner rwx (7), others --- (0).

options.text: Read, write, and execute it; mode 770
options.rationale: The group has no write bit.

options.text: Read it only; mode 740
options.rationale: The group also has execute.

options.text: Nothing; mode 700
options.rationale: The group has read and execute.

questions.explanation: Linux/UNIX permissions are read (4), write (2), and execute (1) for owner, group, and others. rwx = 7, r-x = 5, and --- = 0, so the mode is 750.
questions.discriminator_tested: Three digits = owner, group, others; r=4, w=2, x=1.

questions.stem: A technician plans to update a server's UEFI firmware. Which practice is correct?

options.text: Get the update from the vendor, verify its integrity, and make sure power can't be interrupted during the update
options.rationale: Correct: an interrupted or tampered firmware update can brick the device.

options.text: Download it from any forum mirror, since firmware is all the same
options.rationale: Untrusted sources can deliver tampered firmware.

options.text: Run the update during peak business hours, so problems are noticed quickly
options.rationale: A failure then would take the server down when it's needed most.

options.text: Skip integrity checks, because firmware updates can't harm a device
options.rationale: A bad or interrupted update can leave the device unusable.

questions.explanation: Driver and firmware updates fix bugs and vulnerabilities in drivers and device firmware (BIOS/UEFI, NICs, storage). Get them from the vendor and verify integrity; an interrupted firmware update can brick the device.
questions.discriminator_tested: Get updates from the vendor and verify them; an interrupted firmware update can brick a device.

questions.stem: A clinic still runs medical-device software on Windows 10 PCs, after Windows 10 reached end of support on October 14, 2025. The PCs have antivirus installed. What is the correct response?

options.text: Upgrade, replace, or isolate the PCs, because they no longer receive security patches
options.rationale: Correct: unpatchable systems need one of those three responses.

options.text: Keep using them as they are; antivirus is enough
options.rationale: Antivirus can't fix the OS vulnerabilities that will no longer be patched.

options.text: Keep using them as long as Windows Update says 'up to date'
options.rationale: After end of support, no new security patches arrive, so 'up to date' means nothing.

options.text: Nothing changes; end of support only stops new features
options.rationale: End of support stops security patches too.

questions.explanation: The OS life cycle runs release, mainstream support, extended support, then end of support. After end of support there are no security patches, so systems must be upgraded, replaced, or isolated.
questions.discriminator_tested: After end of support there are no security patches; upgrade, replace, or isolate.

questions.stem: An analyst wants to review failed logon attempts (Event ID 4625) on a Windows server. Which Event Viewer log should they open?

options.text: Security
options.rationale: Correct: logons and audited actions are recorded there.

options.text: System
options.rationale: The System log covers OS components and drivers.

options.text: Application
options.rationale: The Application log covers programs.

options.text: Setup
options.rationale: The Setup log covers installation and update events.

questions.explanation: In Event Viewer, the Security log holds logons and audited actions (Audit Success and Failure, such as 4624 logon and 4625 failed logon). The System log covers OS components and drivers; the Application log covers programs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Security log = logons and audit events.

questions.stem: Why must audit logs be protected from tampering?

options.text: They are the accountability trail of who did what, when, and from where; an attacker who can edit them can erase the evidence
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Tampering slows the server down
options.rationale: Performance isn't the reason.

options.text: Protecting them saves disk space
options.rationale: Protection has nothing to do with storage space.

options.text: They contain every user's password
options.rationale: Audit logs record actions, not passwords.

questions.explanation: Audit logs record security-relevant actions (who, what, when, from where), enabled by audit policy on Windows or auditd on Linux. As the accountability trail, they must be protected from tampering.
questions.discriminator_tested: Audit logs are the accountability trail and must be tamper-protected.

questions.stem: A router sends its log messages to a server on UDP 514. Which statement about this traffic is correct?

options.text: It is standard syslog: cleartext and unreliable; syslog over TCP or TLS (6514) adds reliability and security
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: It is encrypted by default
options.rationale: Syslog over UDP 514 is cleartext.

options.text: Delivery is guaranteed because it uses TCP
options.rationale: UDP has no delivery guarantee.

options.text: These are SNMP traps
options.rationale: SNMP traps use UDP 162.

questions.explanation: Syslog is the standard protocol for sending log messages, by default over UDP 514. That is cleartext and unreliable; TCP or TLS (6514) adds reliability and security.
questions.discriminator_tested: Syslog over UDP 514 is cleartext and unreliable.

questions.stem: After gaining administrator access to a router, an attacker wipes its local logs. Investigators can still reconstruct the attack in order. What made that possible?

options.text: A central syslog collector had already received copies of the logs, with timestamps kept consistent by NTP
options.rationale: Correct: the remote copy survived, and consistent time let events be ordered.

options.text: The router's local log buffer
options.rationale: That is what the attacker wiped.

options.text: Event Viewer on the router
options.rationale: Event Viewer is a Windows tool.

options.text: The router's ACL hit counters
options.rationale: Hit counts don't describe what an attacker did.

questions.explanation: A syslog collector is a central server that receives syslog from many devices. Its copy survives if a device is compromised or wiped, and it needs consistent time (NTP) to correlate events.
questions.discriminator_tested: A central syslog copy survives device compromise; it needs NTP.

questions.stem:
A router logs:

%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down

What does the 3 indicate?

options.text: The severity level: 3, Error
options.rationale: Correct: the number in the middle is the severity.

options.text: The interface number
options.rationale: The interface is named in the description, GigabitEthernet0/1.

options.text: The facility
options.rationale: The facility is LINK, the first field.

options.text: The message sequence number
options.rationale: Sequence numbers come before the timestamp, not inside the %-field.

questions.explanation: Cisco syslog messages use the format %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: description. In %LINK-3-UPDOWN, LINK is the facility, 3 (Error) is the severity, and UPDOWN is the mnemonic.
questions.discriminator_tested: The number in the middle is the severity level.

questions.stem:
A router is configured with:

logging trap 4

Which messages are sent to the syslog server?

options.text: Levels 0 through 4, from Emergency to Warning
options.rationale: Correct: level N sends N and everything more severe.

options.text: Only level 4 (Warning) messages
options.rationale: A level setting includes all more severe levels too.

options.text: Levels 4 through 7, from Warning to Debugging
options.rationale: Higher numbers are less severe; they are excluded.

options.text: Levels 5 through 7 only
options.rationale: Those are the less severe levels that are filtered out.

questions.explanation: Logging severity levels run 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging. A lower number is more severe, and setting level N logs 0 through N.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lower number = more severe; level N logs 0 through N.

questions.stem: Which two log findings are anomalies worth investigating? (Choose two.)

options.text: The Security log on a domain controller was cleared (Event ID 1102)
options.rationale: Correct: clearing the log is a classic way to hide activity.

options.text: 200 failed logons (4625) on one account within five minutes, followed by a success
options.rationale: Correct: this pattern suggests a password attack that worked.

options.text: A user's usual 9 a.m. weekday logon
options.rationale: This matches the baseline.

options.text: The nightly scheduled backup completing
options.rationale: Expected, routine activity.

options.text: Routine Windows Update installs on Patch Tuesday
options.rationale: Expected, scheduled activity.

questions.explanation: Identifying anomalies means comparing log activity with a baseline: off-hours logons, repeated failed logons, new admin accounts, unusual traffic. A cleared Security log (1102) is itself a red flag.
questions.discriminator_tested: Anomalies need a baseline; a cleared Security log is a red flag.

questions.stem: What does a SIEM add that a syslog collector alone does not?

options.text: It normalizes and correlates logs from many sources, with alerts and dashboards
options.rationale: Correct: a collector stores logs; a SIEM analyzes them.

options.text: It only stores logs in one place
options.rationale: Central storage is what a collector already does.

options.text: It encrypts every log so no one can read it
options.rationale: Encryption isn't the defining feature.

options.text: It replaces the network firewall
options.rationale: A SIEM analyzes events; it doesn't filter traffic.

questions.explanation: A SIEM aggregates, normalizes, and correlates logs from many sources, adding alerts, dashboards, and retention. A syslog collector stores logs; a SIEM analyzes them.
questions.discriminator_tested: A collector stores logs; a SIEM correlates them.
